findings.inference: The five profiled workloads are all fit by wall ~= max(H, T) with a single per-call host cost H ~= 98-105 us: timing-16 (T=11.4 us -> wall 97.9), timing-0 (T=5.5 -> 105.2), timing-13 (T=81.5 -> 103.9), timing-2 (T=183.9 -> 184.2), timing-14 (T=317.9 -> 317.5). Only three of the eighteen timing workloads (timing-2, timing-8, timing-14) have latency above H, so only those three currently expose any kernel headroom; the other fifteen measured 0.098-0.108 ms and are dominated by host dispatch per call. Consequence for planning: further kernel-side work can move geo_mean only through timing-2/8/14, and each of those is only 1/18 of the geomean.

findings.inference: Halving the element size (fp32 268 MB -> fp16 134 MB) cut kernel time by 42% (317.9 -> 183.9 us) but barely changed vector busy time (141.5 -> 127.6 us), i.e. the vector stage costs the same per element regardless of width, so it is element-rate work (the R x BK int32 compare plus tl.where select at main.py:69), not byte-rate work. The vector pipe is 69.6% time-active in the fp16 case while MTE3 is only 16.5% active and the vendor reports MTE2/MTE3 below 80% utilisation when active, so the 134 MB of stores are not close to saturating the memory path. fp16 therefore still has headroom that is gated by the select, unlike fp32.

findings.label: fp32 large case: no pipe is saturated (MTE2/MTE3 <80% when active, vector compute usage <20%) while effective write rate is 845 GB/s
findings.backend_detail: Effective rate uses logical output bytes only (no read-modify-write; grad+indices reads are ~0.07 MB). It is not a Roofline claim: physical DRAM bytes and a verified hardware ceiling were not measured, and the 168 MB L2 can absorb the fp16 and smaller outputs.

findings.inference: For fp32 the AIV is busy for essentially the whole kernel (316.5 of 317.9 us) but no individual pipe is close to saturated and arithmetic throughput is under 20% of vector peak, so the kernel is stall/dependency bound rather than limited by any single throughput resource. Two readings remain live: (a) the ~845 GB/s effective write rate is near this device's achievable HBM write rate, so the stores are effectively the wall even though the MTE3 ratio is low; (b) the R=1, single-shot 32 KB tile leaves vector compute and store drain little chance to overlap inside a block. The counters cannot separate these; the select-removal experiment below does, because it lowers vector work while leaving byte volume unchanged.

findings.label: Program count is not an independent limiter: block throughput is constant at 22-26 blocks/us because bytes per block are constant
findings.backend_detail: AIC/AIV counts from the msprof simulator log (24 AIC, num_vec_core=2); the config reports num_sm=20, so wave arithmetic is approximate.

bytes per block (TARGET_BYTES, constant R*BK*elem_size)

findings.inference: Block counts of 8192 down to 256 all land in the same 22-26 blocks/us band; because R is chosen so every block writes exactly 32768 bytes, that band is just a restatement of an ~800-845 GB/s byte rate, so nothing here shows that 8192 programs are inherently expensive. The only grid-shape artefact visible is timing-0, which has 64 blocks over 24 AIC / 48 AIV (1.33 waves) and drops to 382 GB/s, but its kernel is 5.5 us and hidden under the host floor. A block-count change therefore has to be justified by bytes per block (or by overlap), not by grid size alone.

performance_interpretation: Round 2's fusion paid off exactly where the frozen hypothesis predicted and not where it claimed: geo_mean went 0.5905 -> 1.5502 and every floor-bound workload fell to the ~0.098-0.108 ms host-dispatch floor, because removing the second launch removed per-call host cost. The hypothesis's second half ('unmasked contiguous stores restore wide vectorized writes so large workloads become bandwidth bound at ~417 GB/s') is not confirmed: achieved logical write rates are 738-845 GB/s and the store pipes are reported under 80% utilisation when active, while the fp16/bf16 pair is 70% vector-active and costs the same per element as fp32. The per-element select introduced by fusion is now the dominant cost for the three kernel-bound workloads (timing-2, timing-8, timing-14), and it buys nothing at those shapes: at most one element per row is nonzero, so ~65-70M compare and 67M select results are discarded. For fp32 the counters cannot separate 'select compute' from 'store drain', which makes select removal the discriminating test as well as the likely win. Fifteen of eighteen timing workloads are already at the host floor, so no kernel change can move them; the realistic geo_mean ceiling from kernel work in this round is set by timing-2/8/14.

next_experiment.action_description: In the (dim == last, contiguous) branch of value_selecting_reduction_backward main.py, stop materialising the R x BK select at main.py:69. Store a pure zero tile over the identical contiguous range (out_ptr + rows[:,None]*K + cols[None,:]), then write only the surviving nonzeros with a single per-row scatter store tl.store(out_ptr + rows*K + idx, g) (R elements, i.e. 1 element for fp32 and 2 for fp16 at the 8192x8192 shapes), and place tl.debug_barrier() between the two stores so the scatter provably lands after the zero fill. Keep the EVEN/FULLK masks, the R/BK/_TARGET_BYTES derivation and the whole general non-last-dim path byte-for-byte unchanged. Rationale: the output is zeros everywhere except exactly one element per row, so the per-element compare+select is dead work; this is round 1's zero+scatter algorithm re-expressed without the second launch that made it lose, which isolates launch cost from element-rate cost.
next_experiment.expected_impact: Vector work drops from ~2 ops/element over 67.1M elements to a wide zero dup+store. fp16/bf16 (timing-2, timing-8): vector-active 127.6 us -> an estimated 60-70 us, latency an estimated 184 -> 120-150 us, speedup 1.69 -> 2.1-2.7. fp32 (timing-14) is the falsifying case: either ~318 us (unchanged, proving the ~845 GB/s write path is the wall) or an estimated 230-270 us, speedup 2.02 -> 2.4-2.8. timing-13 and the eleven other floor-bound workloads should be unchanged because they sit at the ~100 us host floor. Estimated geo_mean 1.55 -> 1.60-1.66 if fp32 is store-bound, up to ~1.70 if it is not.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Write-after-write hazard: two stores in one program target overlapping addresses and the compiler is not obliged to preserve ordering between them, so the scatter could be overwritten by zeros non-deterministically. Mitigations: tl.debug_barrier() between the stores, plus running the correctness phase twice to catch flakiness (a clean single pass is not sufficient evidence here). Secondary risk: the per-row scatter is a 1-2 element masked MTE3 op per block (8192 extra ops for timing-14) and could itself cost time at the small shapes. Do not touch the general path, the EVEN/FULLK derivation, or dtype/stride semantics, and remove no mask without the existing divisibility conditions. Rollback is trivial because the round-2 file stays on disk: revert to .kernelgen/evals/round-0002/main.py if correctness is flaky or if timing-14 and timing-2/8 do not both improve.
success_criteria: All 96 workloads pass: 78 correctness (run the correctness phase twice to expose store-ordering flakiness) and 18 timing.
timing-2 and timing-8 each fall below 0.160 ms (speedup >= 1.95), i.e. the fp16 vector-bound hypothesis is confirmed.
geo_mean >= 1.60, with no floor-bound workload regressing by more than 2% versus round 2.

timing-14 is recorded either way: if it stays >= 310 us, conclude the ~845 GB/s effective write path is the fp32 wall and stop discarding vector work for fp32; if it drops, re-check whether the remaining limit is store drain.

warnings: Instruction-level collection was requested for timing-2 and timing-14 and failed on both with 'profiling deadline expired during Ascend simulator kernel 0' (simulator ran 446 s for timing-2; artifacts under .kernelgen/profiles/round-0002/.../ebdad92e979a407ebc387ab1e09455d7/ and .../4833e2c44d71403d95976cb6f2efc723/, including timeout.log). The device-level per-kernel reports (PipeUtilization, ArithmeticUtilization, L2Cache, Memory, ResourceConflictRatio, MemoryUB) did complete; only their text Performance Summary is readable here, because the detailed metric tables sit inside msprof-op-report.tar.gz archives that this analysis could not unpack. No instruction listing or source-to-PC mapping was obtained, so the per-element select claim rests on pipe counters and dtype scaling, not on instruction-level evidence.

The detailed op-profiling run reports a longer duration than the metrics run for the same kernel (timing-14: 365.6 us vs 317.9 us; timing-2: 184.1 us vs 183.9 us). All rates above use the metrics run, which matches eval latency; the 365.6 us figure is treated as detailed-profiling perturbation, not as a second measurement of the round.

The vendor 'aivector compute usage lower than 20%' rule hit exists only for timing-14; timing-2 raised only the MTE2/MTE3 rules. Pipe ratios are active-time fractions and are not additive, so 0.4486+0.2853+0.2094+0.2193 must not be read as a 116% time decomposition.

Effective write rates (382-845 GB/s) are logical output bytes divided by kernel time. Physical DRAM bytes, read-for-ownership traffic and a verified device bandwidth ceiling were not measured, so no quantitative Roofline claim is made; the 168 MB L2 can hold the fp16 and all smaller outputs.

Host-side cost H ~= 98-105 us is inferred from kernel-duration vs eval-latency differences plus launch spacing; the execution trace contains only device kernel tasks and HostToDevice flow markers, no host API durations, so the split of H between harness overhead, torch allocation and the Triton launcher is unmeasured.
open_questions: What fraction of the ~100 us per-call host floor belongs to the harness versus to the candidate's own Python path (grad.new_empty, the next_power_of_2/grid arithmetic, and the 13-argument Triton launch)? A host-side instrumentation pass would be needed; if the candidate's share is large, cutting launch overhead would lift fifteen workloads at once and dominate any kernel-side gain.

Is the ~845 GB/s effective write rate at timing-14 the achievable HBM write rate on this Ascend910B4, or an artefact of the R=1 single-shot tile? The select-removal experiment answers this only indirectly.

Would giving each program several row-tiles in a pipelined loop (constant UB footprint, num_stages>1) recover the vector/store overlap that a single-shot 32 KB tile cannot have? Growing R directly is constrained by UB: an fp32 R=1 tile already holds 32 KB of values plus a 32 KB int32 offset tensor.
timing-8 (bf16) was not profiled; its eval latency matches timing-2 to 2 us, so it was treated as a twin rather than an independent regime.
